The petitioner has filed this petition under Section 34(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 and requested this Court to set aside the Arbitral Award dated 10.03.2020 passed in case No.LAQ/ARB/NH- 4/CR/01/2012-13 pertaining to Sy.No.47/1 to an extent of 456 sq. feet by respondent No.2.
A.P. No.106/2021 .2.

It is stated that the Central Government for the purpose of widening of NH-4 on the stretch of land from Kms.10 to Kms.29.50 of Bangalore - Nelamangala section (hereinafter referred to as the project) issued preliminary notification, dated 22nd November 2006.

U/sec.3-A(1)
of the National Highways Act in respect of acquistion of lands situated at Chikkabidrakallu village,
Dasanapura Hobli, Bangalore North taluk, the final notification was published in the official Gazzette on 13th November 2007.

.3. It is stated that under the said notification issued for 1st stage of acquisition, amongst other lands the Agricultural (dry) Lands in Sy.No.47/1 to an extent of 42.3 Sq.Mtrs.equivalent to 456 Sq.ft.,
situated at the said village was also acquired.
It is stated that in accordance with section 3(a) of the NH Act, Respondent no.3 was appointed as the competent authority.

.4. It is stated that the respondent No.3 vide award dated 10th April 2008 determined the market value of Agricultural lands at Rs.25 lakhs per acre A.P. No.106/2021 equivalent to Rs.617.76/- per Sq. Mtr.

In order to determine compensation, the 3rd respondent had procured from the office of the Sub-Registrar, Bangalore North Taluk, the sales statistics from 23rd November 2005 to 22nd November 2006 (preceding one year)and the Guidance Value for the relevant period.

It is stated that in so far as agricultural (dry) lands were concerned, the 3rd respondent observed that the average of the Sales Statistics was Rs.18,11,966/- per acre.
.5.

It is stated that since the guidance value was on higher side, the 3rd respondent relied upon the same and determined the market value of agricultural (dry) lands at Rs.25 lakhs acre equivalent to Rs.617.76/- per sq.mtr.
Being dissatisfied with the amount awarded by respondent no.3 the 1st respondent approached the 2nd respondent U/sec.3-G(5) of the NH Act.

It is stated that the A.P./106/2021 on 14 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/177500737/
2 petitioner entered appearance and filed its statement of objections with documents as well as written submissions.

The 2nd respondent redetermined the market value of agricultural lands at A.P. No.106/2021 Rs.2,43,50,040/- per acre equivalent to Rs.559/- per sq.ft ie the 2nd respondent has enhanced the market value from Rs.25,00,000/-per acre Rs.2,43,50,040/- per acre by treating them as commercial lands abutting national highways.

.6. Being aggrieved by the impugned Arbitral Award, the petitioner has preferred this petition on the following grounds:
a) The impugned Arbitral award passed by the 2nd Respondent is perverse, patently illegal capricious and goes against the very fundamentals of Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996.

b) The 2nd respondent has grossly erred in not following the provisions of NH Act I.e, section 3-G(7)(a).
c) The 2nd Respondent has not complied with the provision of Section 28 of the A &
C Act.
d) The petitioner had specifically contended that the claims of the 1st Respondent were A.P. No.106/2021 barred by time since the award was passed by the 3rd Respondent on 10th April 2008 but the 1st Respondent belatedly approached the 2nd Respondent on 4th October 2012 which was beyond the period of 3 years from the date of passing of award by the 3 rd Respondent.
e) The 2nd respondent has not made any attempt to investigate the market value of subject lands as on the date of publication of preliminary notification.
f) The 2nd respondent abruptly at page 7 of the impugned Arbitral award, has relied upon notification dated 17th April 2007 which came in effect from 19th April 2007.
The notification relied upon the 2 nd respondent came into effect from 19 th April 2007 ie after a lapse of more than 5 months from the date of publication of preliminary notification.
Hence the respondent could not have relied upon the same for the purpose of enhancement compensation.
The 2nd respondent has taken the rate of Rs.1,50,00,000/- per acre.
The 2nd respondent has subtracted the amount awarded by the 3rd respondent and already disbursed I.e Rs. 25 lakhs per acre and arrived at Rs.1,25,00,000/- per acre equivalent to Rs.287/- per sq.

thereafter the 2nd respondent has held that the lands were abutting NH and that the lands acquired were commercial nature on account of which the 1st respondent entitled to an addition of 75% on Rs.287/- per Sq.ft.
A.P./106/2021 on 14 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/177500737/
3 h)
The relevant entry at page No. 288 Sl.no. 15 provides that the guidance value of agricultural lands situated at Chikkabidrakallu village was Rs.42 lakhs per acre.
The entry at the very same page at Sl.No.15(a) provides for guidance value of few sy.nos. abutting NH as Rs.1,50,00,000/- per acre so far as agricultural land is concerned.
The entry at Sl.No.15(a) includes the subject lands.
i) It is pertinent to note that the 2 nd respondent at the most could have taken the A.P. No.106/2021 rate of Rs.42 lakhs per acre and added a percentage of 50 as per the special instructions.
In the alternative the 2 nd respondent could have awarded Rs.1,50,00,000/-per acre which is the guidance value specifically provided for lands abutting NH which covers the subject lands.

j) Further the 2nd respondent without assigning any reasons , in the operative portion of the impugned Arbitral award, has treated the agricultural lands as Commercial lands which is completely arbitrary.
k) It is well settled principle of law that no lands can be treated as unless they are duly converted u/sec.95 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act.
l) The notification dated 17 th April 2007 is a document which did not form a part of Arbitral proceedings.
The 2nd respondent should have brought the same to the notice of the petition before relying upon the same A.P. No.106/2021 which establishes denial of an opportunities to rebut.

m) The 2nd respondent has given the benefit of enhancement to the 1st respondent without production by the 1st respondent of any records or evidence in support of such enhancement which is completely arbitrary.
The impugned arbitral award is not a speaking order and liable to be set aside.
(n) A copy the impugned Arbitral award was received by the petitioner for the first time though the 3rd respondent on 27th November 2020.
Hence the 2nd respondent has violated provision of section 31(5) of the A & C Act.
(o) The petitioner submits that the impugned Arbitral award was passed on 10 th March 2020.

Petition is being filed in accordance with the order passed by the Honble Supreme Court in Suo Moto W.P. (Civil) 3/2020 excluding the period of limitation period A.P. No.106/2021 between 15th March 2020 till 14th March 2021.
Hence, the petition is in time.

.7. The respondent No.1 has filed objections stating that Section 28(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act is not applicable in view of Section 2(6) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
.8.
It is stated that the Apex Court decision Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited Vs. SAW Pipes Ltd (AIR 2003 SC 2629 will not be applicable to this case.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: As per Section 2(6) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 the provisions of Section 28(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act will not apply to this case.

A.P./106/2021 on 14 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/177500737/
4 .9.

With regard to the contention that the respondent No. 2 should have brought the notification to the notice of the petitioner before relying upon the same which establishes denial of an opportunity to the petitioner, it is contended that the Arbitrator is sole arbitrator and so Section 24(1)(2)(3) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act does not apply.
It is stated that even petitioner itself has not filed application before Arbitrator under Section 24 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act.

It is stated that as per Section 2(6)
of Arbitration and Conciliation Act the provisions of Section 28(1)(a) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act will not apply to this case.
.11. It is stated that the Arbitral award is speaking order.

Hence, there was no violation on the side of respondent No. 2 in enhancing award from Rs. 25,00,000/- to Rs. 2,43,50,040/- per acre; that even petitioner itself has not filed application before Arbitrator under Section 24 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
Hence, it is clear that the impugned arbitral award is not opposed to settle position of law.

Hence, payed for dismissal of the suit.
.12.
Perused the written arguments filed by petitioner.

.13. The following points that would arise for my consideration are:
A.P. No.106/2021 (1) Whether the petitioner proves any of the grounds mentioned under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, to set aside the award passed by the learned Arbitrator?
(2) What order or award?
.14.

My findings on the above points are:
Point No.1 : In the affirmative, Point No.2 : As per final order, for the following:
REASONS .15. POINT No.1: The respondent No

. 3 has acquired the agricultural land in Sy.No. 47/1 to an extent of 42.3 sq. meters equivalent to 456 sq. feet situated at Chikkabidarakallu village under the preliminary notification dated 22.11.2006.
The respondent No. 3 has determined the market value of agricultural land at Rs. 25 lakhs per acre equivalent to Rs. 617.76 sq. meters.

The respondent No. 1 being dissatisfied with the award amount had approached the respondent No. 2 under Section 3-G(5)
of NH Act.
The A.P. No.106/2021 respondent No. 2 has re-determined the the market value at Rs. 2,43,50,040/- per acre equivalent to Rs. 502/- per sq. feet.

Being aggrieved by the said award, the petitioner has filed this petition under Section 34 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
.16.
It is necessary to bear in mind the scope of this Court to interfere with the award passed by the Arbitrator.
Section 34(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provide the circumstances under which an award can be set aside by a civil Court.

Explanation shows (1) that an award is in conflict with the pubic policy of India if the making of the award was induced or affected by fraud or corruption or was in violation of Section 75 or Section 81.
(2) It is in conflict with contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian Law or iii) It is in conflict with most basic notion of morality or justice.
Explanation 2.
The test as to whether there is contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law shall not entail a review on the merits of the dispute.

2A It may also be set aside if the Court finds the award is vitiated by patent illegality appearing on the face of award provided that an award shall not be set aside merely on the ground of an erroneous application of law or by re appreciation of evidence.
A.P. No.106/2021
Bearing in mind the above section, now it has to be seen whether the impugned award suffers from any patent error illegality as envisage in the above section.

.17. The respondent No. 1 has contended that the petition filed by the petitioner is hit by provision of Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act since the petition is filed after lapse of 14 months.
The arbitral award was passed on 10.03.2000.
This petition has been filed on 21.05.2021.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Suo-motto case W.P. No. 3/2020 has extended the period of limitation on account of Covid-19.
As, the petition is filed within the extended period of limitation it is in time.

.18. The petitioner has contended that the claim of the respondent No. 1 were barred by time since the award was passed by the respondent No. 3 on 10.04.2008 but the respondent No. 1 belatedly approached the respondent No. 2 on 04.10.2012 which was beyond the period of 3 years from the date of A.P. No.106/2021 passing of the award.

It is stated that the respondent No. 2 has not at all A.P./106/2021 on 14 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/177500737/
6 considered the ground of limitation.
The respondent No. 2 in the award passed has not stated anything with regard to the limitation.

.19. The respondent No. 1 has contended that Section 2(4) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act reads as follows:
" This part, except sub-section (1) of Section 40, sections 41 and 43 shall apply to every arbitration under any other enactment for the time being in force, as if the arbitration were pursuant to an arbitration agreement and as if that other enactment were an arbitration agreement, except insofar as the provisions of this part are inconsistent with that other enactment or with any rules made thereunder".

Hence,
the question of violation of substantive law does not arise by not following the provision of Article 137 of limitation Act."
.20.

The respondent No. 1 advocate has relied upon the decision reported in WP petition No. 13670 of 2021 on 21.04.2022 of Hon'ble High Court of A.P. No.106/2021 Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur,
wherein it is observed that:
"the Parliament in its wisdom has deliberately avoided prescribing a limitation for filing such an appeal.

entities.text: High Court of A.P. No.106/2021 Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The reason may not be too far to find.
It is ultimately the village namely the land owner who loses his land under compulsory acquisition.

Therefore,
to restrict him by limitation from claiming an enhancement, in our considered view,
may not be just or fair, when the landowner has a right to compensation as well as to seek its enhancement, to restrict the same by limitation may lead to gross injustice rather than justice.
The authority would not be benefited if there is no limitation applicable to such cases.

Therefore, it could also be contended that keeping this in mind, the Parliament has deliberately not enforced any limitation for exercise of such aright and on the other hand, it cannot be said that there was an omission by the Parliament to do so.
Secondly, even assuming that Article 137 of the Limitation Act would stand applicable, in that event the powers of the court under Section 5 of the Limitation Act will come into play.
The National Highways Act does not specifically bar the provisions of Section 5 of the Limitation Act.

Therefore,even if it is to be held that Article 137 is to be applied, then the delay in filing such an appeal would require to be considered in exercise of the powers under Section 5 of the Limitation Act A.P.
No.106/2021 based on the facts and circumstances involved and sufficiency of cause.
.21.

The petitioner has relied upon Section 34 of the NH Act, which reads as under:
As per Section 3G(5) of the National Highways Act which reads as under:
"3G(5) - If the amount determined by the competent authority under Sub Section (1)
or Sub Section (2) is not acceptable to either of the parties, the amount shall, on an application by either of the parties, be determined by the Arbitrator to be appointed by the Central Government."
A.P./106/2021 on 14 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/177500737/
7 .22.

In W.A. No. 31066/2012 & 31094-96/2012 (T. Yunis Vs. National Highways Authority of India and others), wherein our Hon'ble High Court has held that:
"No period of limitation has been stipulated to seek a reference under Section 3G(5)
of the National Highways Act. In such circumstances, the only provision available to the parties is to invoke Article 137 of the Limitation Act, which provides three years from the date on which right to apply accrues".

entities.text: W.A. No. 31066/2012 & 31094-96/2012 (T. Yunis Vs. National Highways Authority of India and others)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The said decision applies to the case on hand.

. In W.A. No. 226/2015 (Leela K Vs. District Collector and Aribtrator and others), the Hon'ble High Court of Kerala has held that:
" Section 3G-Application for arbitration under Section 3G(5) should be filed within three years from the date on which the compensation is determined by the competent authority and intimated to the land owner."

entities.text: W.A. No. 226/2015 (Leela K Vs. District Collector and Aribtrator and others)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The said decision applies to the case on hand.
.24. The contention of the respondent No. 1 that the limitation is not applicable cannot be accepted in view of the above decision.
On perusal of the record, it is seen that the record does not contain the date when the notice of the award has been served to the respondent No. 1.
The award is not published in the Gazette.
The land loosers will not be aware about the date of passing of the award.
Issuance of notice to person interested in award immediately on making of award is mandatory.

Mere disbursal of amount to awardee after obtaining his signature or thumb impression on voucher does not constitute notice of A.P.
No.106/2021 award.
It is only when the notice is served to the land owners/ land loosers the period of limitation begins.
The records do not disclose the date of service of notice.
In the absence of materials it is not proper to say that the petition is barred by limitation.
The petitioner can produce the same before Arbitrator and can take up the contention with regard to limitation.
.25. The petitioner has stated that the respondent No.3 Arbitrator has relied upon the notification dated 17.04.2007 which came into effect from 19.04.2007.
Preliminary notification in the present case was issued on 20.11.2006.

It is stated that as per Substantial Law NH Authority Act Section 3-G(7)(a), the arbitrator while determining the amount shall take into consideration the market value of the land as on the date of publication of the notification under Section 3-A of NH Act.
It is argued that the respondent No.2 could not have relied upon the guidelines value which came into effect after publication of preliminary notification dated 20.11.2006.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Oil & Natural Gas Corp. Ltd., Vs. SAW Pipes Ltd. (AIR 2003 SC 2629) has held that:
 "if the award is contrary to the  Substantive provisions of law or the provisions of the Act or against the terms of the contract, it would be patently illegal, which could be interfered under Section 34".
A.P./106/2021 on 14 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/177500737/
8

entities.text: Oil & Natural Gas Corp. Ltd., Vs. SAW Pipes Ltd. (AIR 2003 SC 2629)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The above decision applies to the case on hand.
.27. If at all the Arbitrator relied on the notification dated 17.04.2007, the respondent No. 2 should have deescalated the value to the date of preliminary notification.
.28. The respondent No. 1 has stated that the decision Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd Vs. SAW Pipes Ltd AIR 2003 SC 2629 Will not be applicable to the case on hand.

entities.text: Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd Vs. SAW Pipes Ltd AIR 2003 SC 2629
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The respondent No. 1 advocate argued that as per Section 2(6) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act the provisions of Section 28(1)(a) of the A.P. No.106/2021 Arbitration and Conciliation Act is not applicable to this case.

As per Sector 2(6) provides that:
"Where this part, except Section 28, leaves the parties free to determine a certain issue, that freedom shall include the right of the parties to authorize any person including an institution, to determine that issue."
From reading of Section 2(6) it is clear that the parties are free to determine certain issue.

However,
it is not applicable to Section 28.
The rules prescribed under Section 28 is mandatory.
In view of the said provisions, the contention of the respondent No. 1 is not sustainable.
.29. The Arbitrator relying upon the guidelines value dated 17.04.2007 has redetermined the market value at Rs. 502/- per sq. feet.

The petitioner has stated that the guidance value of agricultural land situated at Chikkabidarakallu village was Rs. 1,50,00,000/- per acre, NA lands was Rs. 425/- per sq. feet an that of gramathana was Rs. 350/- per sq. feet.

In order to re-determine the market value for agricultural lands, the respondent No. 2 has taken the rate of Rs. 1,50,00,000/- per acre and thereafter subtracted the amount awarded by the respondent No. 3 and has arrived at Rs.
1,25,00,000/- per acre equivalent to Rs. 287/- per sq. feet.

Thereafter, has held that the lands were abutting NH and that the lands acquired were commercial in nature on account of which the respondent No. 1 is entitled to addition of A.P. No.106/2021 75% on Rs. 287/- per sq. feet and arrived at Rs. 502/- per sq. feet.

Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/177500737/
9 provides that the guidance value of Sy.No. 47 abutting NH as Rs. 1,50,00,000/- per acre.

The special instruction to the said notification provides that a percentage of 50 and 25 is to be added on the guidance for lands abutting NH and State Highway respectively when the guidance value of particular property is not specifically provided for under the notification.
The L.A.O. apart from taking guidance value of lands abutting to NH a sum of Rs. 1,50,00,000/- per acre, in addition has added rate fixed for lands abutting to NH 50% and for commercial lands as 50%.
The Arbitrator has not given reasons as to why he has treated the land as commercial land and has fixed the market value.
.32. There is no indication to the manner in which notification dated 17.04.2007 was brought on record though the said notification was published in the Gazette.
Necessary pleading in claim petition and A.P. No.106/2021 evidence with opportunity to NHAI to rebut should have been placed before the learned Arbitrator.
Based on the same the learned Arbitrator ought to have arrived at conclusion with regard to the applicability of guidance value.
Necessary evidence to derive comparison between the lands.

So as to apply the value fixed in-respect of commercial lands in the same notification was necessary to be brought on record and was to be considered by the respondent No. 2 - Arbitrator by assigning reasons.
The Arbitrator has not referred to the manner in which notification dated 17.04.2007 was brought on record and relied in the proceedings.
The value for the acquired land was fixed in the notification by specifying the survey number.
The respondent No. 2 ought to have given necessary reason to have considered the land as commercial land in the absence of any document produced by respondent No. 1.

The award would indicate that the respondent No. 1 did not have sufficient opportunity before the Arbitrator to controvert the material sought to be relied upon by the A.P. No.106/2021 respondent No. 2 nor the respondent No. 2 Arbitrator indicated sufficient reasons which to that extent would indicate patent illegality in the award passed by the respondent No.2 being contrary to Section 28(2) and 31(3) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
.33.
The Arbitrator has relied upon guidelines value dated 17.04.2007.
This document is not valid record received from the Arbitrator as none of the parties have produced and this is evident from the record of the Arbitrator.
Section 24(3) of the Act provides provision regarding hearing and written proceedings.

It reads thus:
"All statements, documents or other information supplied to, or applications made to the aribral tribunal by one party shall be communicated to the other party, and any expert report or evidentiary document on which the arbital tribunal may rely in making its decision shall be communicated to the parties".
.34.
The respondent No. 1 has contended that the provisions of Section 24(1)(2)(3) of the Arbitration and A.P. No.106/2021 Conciliation Act does not apply to Arbitrator as he is sole Arbitrator.

The provisions of Section 24 is clear that unless other wise agreed by the parties, the Arbitral Tribunal shall decide whether to hold oral hearings for the presentation of evidence or for oral argument, or whether the proceedings shall be conducted on the basis of documents and other materials.
In the present case there is no agreement between the parties.
In the absence of agreement the provisions of Section 24 is applicable to sole arbitrator also.

A.P./106/2021 on 14 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/177500737/
10 .35.

As the Arbitrator has relied on the estimated guidelines value of immovable properties and buildings dated 17.04.2007 without bringing to the knowledge of the parties and thereby has failed to follow the procedure under Section 24 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.

So the award has to be set aside on the ground of patent illegality.
.36.

The petitioner has contended that the respondent No.2 has not assigned any reasons for re- determining the compensation nor he has assigned any A.P. No.106/2021 reasons for enhancing the compensation or for relying upon notification dated 17.04.2007.
.37.

In Som Dutt Builders Ltd Vs. State of Kerala (2010)2 AWC (supp) 1390 SC) has held that:
"Reasons must be indicated in the award as that would reflect thought process leading to a particular conclusion.

entities.text: Som Dutt Builders Ltd Vs. State of Kerala (2010)2 AWC (supp) 1390 SC)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: To satisfy the requirement of Section 31(3), the reasons must be stated by the Arbitral Tribunal upon which the award is based; want of reasons would make such award legally flawed."

.38. On perusal of the records and the award of the Arbitrator it is seen that the respondent No.2 has neither complied with the procedure provided under Section 24 nor decided the dispute in accordance with Section 28(1)(a) and at the same time has failed to comply with Section 31(3) of the A & C Act, thus rendering the impugned Arbitral Award opposed to settled position of law.

.39. The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Oil & Natural Gas Corp. Ltd. Vs. SAW Piles Ltd., (AIR 2003 SC 2629) has held that:
A.P. No.106/2021 "if the award is patently against the statutory provisions of Substantive law which is in force in India or is passed without giving an opportunity of hearing to the parties as provided under Section 24 or without giving any reason in a case where parties have not agreed that no reasons are to be recorded, it would be against the statutory provisions.

entities.text: Oil & Natural Gas Corp. Ltd. Vs. SAW Piles Ltd., (AIR 2003 SC 2629)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In all such cases, the award is required to be set aside on the ground of 'patent illegality'
The above decision is applies to the case in hand.
In view of the above discussion, I answer point No.1 in the affirmative.
.40. Point No.2:

In view of the aforesaid finding on point No.1 I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER A.P. No.106/2021 is allowed.

The impugned award passed by the respondent No.2 in so far as pertaining to case No.LAQ/ARB/NH- 4/CR/01/2012-13 is set aside with a liberty to the parties to pursue their remedy in accordance with law.

b) The 2nd respondent has grossly erred in not following the provisions of NH Act I.e, section 3-G(7)(a).

d) The petitioner had specifically contended that the claims of the 1st Respondent were A.P. No.106/2021 barred by time since the award was passed by the 3rd Respondent on 10th April 2008 but the 1st Respondent belatedly approached the 2nd Respondent on 4th October 2012 which was beyond the period of 3 years from the date of passing of award by the 3 rd Respondent.
j) Further the 2nd respondent without assigning any reasons , in the operative portion of the impugned Arbitral award, has treated the agricultural lands as Commercial lands which is completely arbitrary.
k) It is well settled principle of law that no lands can be treated as unless they are duly converted u/sec.95 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act.
l) The notification dated 17 th April 2007 is a document which did not form a part of Arbitral proceedings.
The 2nd respondent should have brought the same to the notice of the petition before relying upon the same A.P. No.106/2021 which establishes denial of an opportunities to rebut.
Hence the 2nd respondent has violated provision of section 31(5) of the A & C Act.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
m) The 2nd respondent has given the benefit of enhancement to the 1st respondent without production by the 1st respondent of any records or evidence in support of such enhancement which is completely arbitrary.
The impugned arbitral award is not a speaking order and liable to be set aside.
The test as to whether there is contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law shall not entail a review on the merits of the dispute.
Therefore,even if it is to be held that Article 137 is to be applied, then the delay in filing such an appeal would require to be considered in exercise of the powers under Section 5 of the Limitation Act A.P.
No.106/2021 based on the facts and circumstances involved and sufficiency of cause.
.21.
The award is not published in the Gazette.
The land loosers will not be aware about the date of passing of the award.
Issuance of notice to person interested in award immediately on making of award is mandatory.
Mere disbursal of amount to awardee after obtaining his signature or thumb impression on voucher does not constitute notice of A.P.
No.106/2021 award.
It is only when the notice is served to the land owners/ land loosers the period of limitation begins.
The records do not disclose the date of service of notice.
In the absence of materials it is not proper to say that the petition is barred by limitation.
.28. The respondent No. 1 has stated that the decision Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd Vs. SAW Pipes Ltd AIR 2003 SC 2629 Will not be applicable to the case on hand.
From reading of Section 2(6) it is clear that the parties are free to determine certain issue.
Based on the same the learned Arbitrator ought to have arrived at conclusion with regard to the applicability of guidance value.
So as to apply the value fixed in-respect of commercial lands in the same notification was necessary to be brought on record and was to be considered by the respondent No. 2 - Arbitrator by assigning reasons.
The Arbitrator has not referred to the manner in which notification dated 17.04.2007 was brought on record and relied in the proceedings.
The value for the acquired land was fixed in the notification by specifying the survey number.
The respondent No. 2 ought to have given necessary reason to have considered the land as commercial land in the absence of any document produced by respondent No. 1.
The award would indicate that the respondent No. 1 did not have sufficient opportunity before the Arbitrator to controvert the material sought to be relied upon by the A.P. No.106/2021 respondent No. 2 nor the respondent No. 2 Arbitrator indicated sufficient reasons which to that extent would indicate patent illegality in the award passed by the respondent No.2 being contrary to Section 28(2) and 31(3) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
